checks.title: EOP preset security policy assigned to everyone
checks.remediation: Turn on the Standard or Strict preset security policy for Exchange Online Protection and leave the recipient scope empty so it applies to all users and domains. Custom policies then exist only for documented exceptions.

userImpact.text: More suspicious mail goes to quarantine; users get a quarantine notice for the mail they might want.

checks.narrative: Preset policies carry Microsoft's recommended anti-spam, anti-malware and anti-phishing settings and update as the recommendations change. A tenant on hand-tuned custom policies drifts; one on the preset with no scope restrictions is protected by default.

checks.title: Defender for Office 365 preset policy assigned to everyone
checks.remediation: Turn on the Standard or Strict preset for Defender for Office 365 with an empty recipient scope, so Safe Links and Safe Attachments reach every mailbox.

userImpact.text: Links in mail are checked when clicked, and some attachments arrive a minute later after scanning.

checks.narrative: The MDO half of the preset is a separate rule. Tenants often enable the EOP preset and never the MDO one, which leaves Safe Links and Safe Attachments on custom policies or off.

checks.title: Anti-phishing: spoof intelligence on and DMARC honoured
checks.remediation: In every enabled anti-phishing policy turn on spoof intelligence and set the DMARC policy to be honoured (reject or quarantine per the sender's record).

userImpact.text: Mail that fails the sender's DMARC policy is quarantined or rejected instead of delivered.

checks.narrative: Spoof intelligence catches senders using your domains or trusted partners' domains without authorisation. Honouring DMARC applies the sender's own published policy instead of the tenant's spam verdict.

checks.title: Impersonation protection for executives and owned domains
checks.remediation: In each anti-phishing policy enable user impersonation protection with the executives and finance roles listed, domain impersonation for the owned domains, and mailbox intelligence.

userImpact.text: Mail impersonating executives or your domains gets a warning tip or goes to quarantine.

checks.narrative: Business email compromise starts with a lookalike display name or domain. Impersonation protection needs the names it should protect; a policy with an empty list protects nobody.

checks.title: Safe Links and Safe Attachments on for mail, Teams and Office
remediation: Enable Safe Links for email, Teams and Office apps in at least one policy.
Enable Safe Attachments with Block or Dynamic Delivery.
In the global settings, turn on Safe Attachments for SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams, and Safe Documents where the licence (E5 or Defender for Endpoint P2) includes it.

userImpact.text: Links are checked when clicked in mail, Teams and Office; attachments are scanned before delivery.

checks.narrative: URL rewriting and detonation at click time, plus attachment detonation, are the controls that stop the payload after the lure got through. Each needs its own policy switch.

checks.title: Zero-hour auto purge for spam, phish and malware
checks.remediation: Enable ZAP in every anti-spam policy (spam and phish) and every anti-malware policy.

userImpact.text: Messages found to be malicious after delivery disappear from the inbox into quarantine.

checks.narrative: ZAP retroactively moves messages already delivered once the verdict changes. Off, a message that was clean at delivery and malicious an hour later stays in the inbox.

checks.title: Quarantine: admin-only release for high-confidence phish, user notifications on
checks.remediation: Set the high-confidence phish quarantine tag to AdminOnlyAccessPolicy in every anti-spam policy and enable end-user quarantine notifications in a quarantine policy.

userImpact.text: Users cannot release high-confidence phishing themselves and get a notice of what was held.

checks.narrative: A user who can release high-confidence phish to themselves defeats the filter. Notifications let users request release of legitimate mail without an admin.

checks.title: Automatic external forwarding blocked
remediation: Set automatic forwarding to Off in the default outbound spam policy and every custom one.
Allow it per user only through a scoped custom policy with a documented reason.

userImpact.text: Users with rules forwarding mail outside the organisation find the forwarding stops.

checks.narrative: Attackers who get a mailbox set a forward and read quietly for months. Blocking it at the tenant level stops both inbox rules and mailbox forwarding from leaving the tenant.

checks.title: Connection filter IP allow list empty
checks.remediation: Remove allow-listed IPs or record each with an owner and reason as an object-level exception. Prefer Enhanced Filtering for a gateway and partner connectors for application senders.

userImpact.text: Mail flow is unchanged for legitimate senders; mail from removed IPs is filtered like any other.

checks.narrative: An IP on the allow list skips spam filtering entirely. Legacy entries for a long-gone gateway or a shared cloud range are an open door.

checks.title: No unscoped SCL -1 transport rules
checks.remediation: Delete bypass rules that no longer have a purpose, and scope the rest to a sender IP range or a header the authenticated connector stamps.

userImpact.text: Mail flow is unchanged; mail that skipped filtering is now filtered.

checks.narrative: A rule that sets SCL -1 on all mail from a domain or a scope turns filtering off for anything that claims to come from it. Spoofed senders pass straight through.

checks.title: Enhanced Filtering on every partner inbound connector
checks.remediation: On each partner connector that fronts the tenant (a third-party gateway), enable Enhanced Filtering with the gateway's IPs so EOP sees the true source.

userImpact.text: Filtering gets more accurate; users notice less spam and fewer false positives.

checks.narrative: With a gateway in front, every message arrives from the gateway's IP, SPF fails and spoof intelligence is blind. Enhanced Filtering restores the original connecting IP.

checks.title: DKIM signing enabled on every custom domain
remediation: Publish the two selector CNAMEs for each custom domain.
Enable DKIM signing for the domain.
Rotate the keys on a schedule.

userImpact.text: Outbound mail is signed; recipients see nothing different.

checks.narrative: DKIM proves the message body was sent by the domain owner's infrastructure and survives forwarding, which SPF does not. DMARC alignment on outbound mail depends on it.

checks.title: DMARC at the target policy with reporting
remediation: Publish _dmarc.<domain> at p=none with an rua address that someone reads, and fix the senders the reports show failing.
Move to p=quarantine as a dated step, with the threshold lowered in the profile until then.
Move to p=reject.

userImpact.text: Mail spoofing your domain is rejected; a forgotten third-party sender may need adding to SPF or DKIM first.

checks.narrative: DMARC tells receivers what to do with mail that fails SPF and DKIM alignment. p=none is monitoring only; without rua nobody sees the reports.

checks.title: SPF valid, under the lookup limit, hard fail
checks.remediation: Publish one SPF record per domain that lists the real senders, stays under ten DNS lookups, and ends with -all. Flatten includes if the count is close.

userImpact.text: A third-party service not listed in SPF may have its mail rejected; list every sender first.

checks.narrative: SPF names the servers allowed to send for the domain. ~all asks receivers to be lenient; more than ten lookups makes the record permanently fail evaluation. The lookup count here is the top-level record only.

checks.title: MTA-STS and TLS-RPT published
checks.remediation: Publish _mta-sts.<domain> with the policy file hosted at https://mta-sts.<domain>/.well-known/mta-sts.txt, and _smtp._tls.<domain> with a reporting address.

userImpact.text: Mail between servers uses enforced encryption; users see nothing.

checks.narrative: MTA-STS makes senders refuse to deliver to the domain without a valid TLS connection, closing the downgrade. TLS-RPT is how failures get reported.

checks.title: No mailboxes forwarding externally
checks.remediation: Clear ForwardingSmtpAddress on mailboxes that should not forward, and record the approved ones as object-level exceptions with an owner.

userImpact.text: Mailboxes stop forwarding outside; their owners read the mail in their own mailbox.

checks.narrative: Mailbox-level forwarding is the second place an attacker persists after inbox rules. Forwarding to a recipient object is listed for verification because the target can be an external contact.

checks.title: Legacy protocols off: SMTP AUTH org-wide, POP and IMAP per mailbox
remediation: Disable SMTP AUTH in the transport config and re-enable it per mailbox only for devices that need it.
Disable POP and IMAP on every mailbox. A new mailbox has both on by default, so set the default plan or run a scheduled job.

userImpact.text: Devices and apps that send by basic SMTP AUTH, POP or IMAP stop working until moved to modern sign-in or a connector.

checks.narrative: Basic authentication for these protocols is retired, but the protocols themselves still work with modern auth and bypass the clients Conditional Access expects. SMTP AUTH is the one that still accepts a password.

checks.title: Shared mailboxes blocked from sign-in
checks.remediation: Block sign-in on the user account behind every shared mailbox. Access goes through delegation, never a password.

userImpact.text: People keep using shared mailboxes through delegation as before.

checks.narrative: The account behind a shared mailbox is created enabled with a random password. Enabled, it is a licence-free, usually MFA-free account anyone who resets the password can use.

checks.title: Mailbox auditing on and the unified audit log enabled
checks.remediation: Enable unified audit log ingestion and keep AuditDisabled false in the organisation config so mailbox auditing applies to every mailbox by default.

userImpact.text: Logging users never see.

checks.narrative: Without the audit log there is no investigation: who read, moved or forwarded what. Mailbox auditing is on by default only while the organisation switch stays off.

checks.title: Attack simulation campaign in the last 90 days
checks.remediation: Run a simulation from Attack simulation training at least quarterly and assign training to the users who click.

userImpact.text: Users receive a simulated phishing mail, and those who click get short training.

checks.narrative: Users are the last filter. A tenant with the licence and no campaigns has the tooling and not the practice.

checks.title: ARC trusted sealers configured for the gateway
checks.remediation: Add the gateway's ARC sealing domain to the trusted ARC sealers list so authentication results survive the hop through it.

userImpact.text: Mail through the gateway is filtered more accurately; users see nothing.

checks.narrative: A gateway that modifies mail breaks DKIM and SPF for the next hop. ARC lets the gateway vouch for the original results; the tenant has to trust the sealer for that to count.

checks.title: A mailbox sending spam is stopped, not only reported
remediation: Set When a user exceeds the limits to Restrict the user from sending mail in each outbound spam policy listed, or turn on the Standard or Strict preset (EM-001).
Keep the alert policy User restricted from sending email so an administrator hears about it.

userImpact.text: People notice nothing unless their mailbox is compromised and starts sending spam, when it stops sending until an admin releases it.

checks.narrative: A compromised mailbox is used to send phishing to customers and partners from a trusted address. Restricting the sender at the limit stops the damage within minutes; only alerting lets it carry on until someone reads the alert.

checks.title: Common attachment filter on in every anti-malware policy
remediation: In each anti-malware policy listed, turn on Enable the common attachments filter and keep Microsoft's default list of file types, adding any your business never receives.

userImpact.text: Attachments of risky file types (scripts, executables, disk images) are quarantined instead of delivered.

checks.narrative: Most malware arrives as a file type nobody needs by email: scripts, executables, disk images and shortcut files. The common attachment filter blocks those by type before any scanning has to recognise them.

checks.title: Partner connectors accept mail only from the partner
remediation: Edit each inbound partner connector listed and require the partner's IP addresses or a TLS certificate subject name matching the partner.
Remove connectors for partners you no longer exchange mail with.

userImpact.text: Mail from the partner flows as before; nobody else can send through the connector.

checks.narrative: A partner connector that accepts any sender address or certificate gives anyone who can send from the partner's domain name the trust meant for the partner, including skipping some filtering. Restricting it to the partner's addresses or certificate keeps the trust where it belongs.

checks.title: Exchange Online PowerShell only for administrators
remediation: Turn it off for everyone who is not an administrator: Get-User -ResultSize Unlimited -Filter "RemotePowerShellEnabled -eq 'True'" | Where-Object { the account is not an admin } | Set-User -RemotePowerShellEnabled $false.
Turn it off for new accounts too, as part of account creation, since it is on by default.
Or close the Exchange Online PowerShell app to everyone but an assigned group (ID-023), which covers new accounts without a script.

userImpact.text: No one who is not an administrator uses Exchange Online PowerShell; Outlook, the web and mobile mail work exactly as before.

checks.narrative: Exchange Online PowerShell is on for every account unless someone turns it off. An ordinary mailbox user can connect to it and read their own mailbox rules, forwarding and permissions at scale, and an attacker with that user's password or token can do the same, including creating inbox rules that hide replies. Administrators need it; nobody else does.

checks.title: Mail arrives only through the email gateway
remediation: Create (or edit) an inbound connector from Partner organization, for sender domains *, that rejects mail unless it comes from the gateway's IP addresses, or from its TLS certificate name.
Take the gateway's published IP ranges or certificate name from the vendor's documentation (Proofpoint, Mimecast and others publish both), and keep them current.
Test by sending straight to the domain's tenant.mail.protection.outlook.com host from outside: the message should be refused.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people: mail still arrives through the gateway as before; only mail that tried to go around it is refused.

checks.narrative: With Proofpoint, Mimecast or another gateway in front of Microsoft 365, the MX record points at the gateway, but Exchange Online still accepts mail sent straight to the tenant's own mail host, which anyone can look up. Attackers send there to skip the gateway's filtering entirely. A partner connector that accepts mail only from the gateway closes that path.

checks.title: Safe Attachments and Safe Links for SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams and Office apps
remediation: In Microsoft Defender, Email and collaboration, Policies, Safe Attachments, Global settings, turn on Defender for Office 365 for SharePoint, OneDrive and Microsoft Teams.
In the Safe Links policy that covers everyone (or the preset policy), turn on Safe Links for Microsoft Teams and for Office 365 apps.
Keep these on even with another email gateway in front: the gateway filters mail, not files shared in SharePoint, OneDrive or Teams.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people unless a file or link is malicious: then the file is blocked or the link opens a warning page.

checks.narrative: A third-party email gateway filters mail, so a check that counts it as covering Defender for Office 365 is right for mail and wrong for everything else. Files shared in SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams, and links clicked in Teams chats and Office documents, reach people without passing the gateway. These settings come with the Defender for Office 365 licence and protect exactly that part.

checks.title: Direct Send is rejected
remediation: Find what sends mail to your own domains without signing in: printers, scanners, line-of-business applications and outside services that send as your domain.
Give each one a way that still works: SMTP client submission with a mailbox, or a partner inbound connector that matches its certificate or its address.
Then turn Direct Send off: Set-OrganizationConfig -RejectDirectSend $true. It takes about half an hour to apply.
Watch the message trace for rejected mail for a week and add a connector for anything that was missed.

userImpact.text: A printer or application that sends unauthenticated mail as your own domain with no connector stops delivering until it has one.

checks.narrative: Direct Send lets anything on the internet hand mail to your tenant's own endpoint with no sign-in, saying it is from one of your own addresses. It was meant for printers. It is also how a message that claims to be from your finance director reaches a mailbox without passing your sender checks the way outside mail does. With it rejected, mail from your own domains has to come through a connector or a signed-in sender.
